cards.q: What happens when kernel-mode code crashes?
cards.a:
The whole machine stops with a bug check (blue screen), because there is nothing above the kernel to recover

A crashing user-mode program is cleaned up by the kernel. A crash in the kernel has nothing above it to clean up, so Windows stops everything to avoid further damage.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: How does user-mode code get something done that only the kernel can do?
cards.a:
It makes a system call, which switches the processor to kernel mode to run trusted code on its behalf

User-mode code cannot jump into kernel code. A system call is the controlled door: the processor changes privilege level and runs only the kernel's own handler. Being an administrator does not change the processor mode.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: Why must all driver testing happen in a virtual machine?
cards.a:
A driver bug can crash or corrupt the whole system

The machine you test on will crash, possibly with corrupted files. In a virtual machine with snapshots that costs a snapshot restore, not your work.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: Why does the VM need more than one virtual processor?
cards.a:
Many race bugs appear only on several processors at once

With one processor, two pieces of code never really run at the same time, so synchronisation bugs between them may never show up in testing.

cards.q: Where is test signing turned on, and why only there?
cards.a:
Only in the target VM, a machine meant to be crashed

Test signing is a development setting that lets test-signed drivers load. Loosening that protection is fine on a throwaway VM; your everyday machine keeps the normal driver signing rules.

cards.q: What does the kernel debugger do when the target crashes?
cards.a:
It stops at the bug check, before the blue screen

With a kernel debugger attached, the bug check breaks into the debugger first, with the machine frozen exactly at the crash, so you can analyse it with commands such as `!analyze -v`.

cards.q: What is the difference between WDM and KMDF?
cards.a:
KMDF is a framework built on top of the WDM model

Every driver ends up as WDM underneath. KMDF wraps the hard, error-prone parts, such as power management and IRP handling, and gets the boilerplate right. User-mode drivers are UMDF, a different framework.

cards.q: In what unit is `UNICODE_STRING`'s `Length` measured?
cards.a:
In bytes, not characters, and without any terminating null

`Length` is a byte count of the text, so `L"abc"` has a `Length` of 6. The buffer is not required to be null-terminated at all.

cards.q: How do you test whether an `NTSTATUS` means success?
cards.a:
`NT_SUCCESS(status)`, which is true for `status >= 0`

Several statuses besides `STATUS_SUCCESS` (0) are successes, such as `STATUS_PENDING`. Errors have the top bit set, which makes them negative as a signed number.

cards.q: What happens if a driver does not set `DriverUnload`?
cards.a:
It cannot be unloaded; it stays until the machine restarts

Without an Unload routine, the kernel has no safe way to remove the driver, so `sc stop` fails and the driver stays loaded.

cards.q: What must `DriverEntry` do before returning a failure status?
cards.a:
Undo everything it already did, because Unload will not run

A driver that fails to load is removed without calling Unload. Anything it created or registered before failing would be leaked or left pointing at freed code.

cards.q: Why is a callback left registered after unload so dangerous?
cards.a:
The kernel later calls code that is no longer there

Unloading frees the driver's image, but the kernel still holds the callback's address. The next event jumps into freed memory and crashes the machine.

cards.q: Why does WinDbg need the driver's `.pdb` file?
cards.a:
It holds the symbols: function names, types and source lines for the driver's code

Without symbols the debugger shows bare addresses. The PDB lets it show your function names, structures and the source line you are on.

cards.q: What does bug check `0xD1` usually mean?
cards.a:
Code at a raised IRQL touched pageable or invalid memory

`0xD1` is `DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL`: at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` or above, page faults cannot be handled, so touching paged-out or invalid memory stops the machine.

cards.q: What is the difference between `bp` and `bu`?
cards.a:
`bu` resolves its name when the module loads, so it can be set early

`bp` needs the address now, so it fails for a driver that is not loaded yet. `bu` keeps the symbolic name and sets the breakpoint when the module appears.

cards.q: Why does a driver create a symbolic link?
cards.a:
User mode cannot open names under `\Device`; the link in `\??` makes the device reachable as `\\.\Name`

Win32 paths are looked up in the `\??` directory. A symbolic link there pointing at `\Device\Name` is what makes `CreateFile(L"\\\\.\\Name")` find the device.

cards.q: What does `IoCreateDeviceSecure` add over `IoCreateDevice`?
cards.a:
A security descriptor saying who may open the device

The SDDL string passed to it decides which accounts, for example SYSTEM and Administrators, can open the device. Exclusivity is a separate flag that works with either function.

cards.q: In which order does Unload delete the link and the device?
cards.a:
The reverse of creation: the symbolic link first, then the device object

Undo in reverse order. Deleting the device first would leave a link that points at a device that no longer exists, and the kernel does not delete your link for you.

cards.q: What does `IoStatus.Information` usually hold?
cards.a:
The number of bytes transferred

The status goes in `IoStatus.Status`. `Information` is the byte count that user mode sees as the result of `ReadFile` or `WriteFile`.

cards.q: What happens if a driver never completes an IRP?
cards.a:
The requesting thread waits forever, and its process cannot exit

Nothing completes an IRP for you. A synchronous caller blocks for good, and the process hangs on exit because its I/O is still outstanding.

cards.q: Why must a driver not touch an IRP after `IoCompleteRequest`?
cards.a:
The IRP may already be freed and reused

Once completed, the IRP belongs to the I/O manager again and can be freed at once, so read anything you need before completing it. Reading it afterwards is a use after free.

cards.q: What does the access field of a control code do?
cards.a:
Makes the I/O manager check the handle's access first

A code with `FILE_WRITE_ACCESS` fails for a handle opened read-only, before your driver sees it. The buffering method is a different field, and who may open the device is set by its security descriptor.

cards.q: Why do driver and client share one header?
cards.a:
They must agree exactly on the control codes and the layout of the data they exchange

The client and driver are built separately. One shared definition of each code and structure means they cannot drift apart.

cards.q: What does the user see as "bytes returned" from `DeviceIoControl`?
cards.a:
The IRP's `IoStatus.Information` value set by the driver

The driver decides how many output bytes are valid by setting `Information`, and the I/O manager reports exactly that to the client.

cards.q: With `METHOD_BUFFERED`, how big is the system buffer for an IOCTL?
cards.a:
The larger of the input and output lengths

The I/O manager allocates one buffer big enough for either, copies the input in, and copies the output back out from the same buffer. Writing output can overwrite input you have not read yet.

cards.q: What does an MDL describe?
cards.a:
The locked physical pages of a user's buffer

A memory descriptor list records which physical pages back the user's buffer, locked so they cannot be paged out. For direct I/O the driver maps them into kernel space.

cards.q: Why is `METHOD_NEITHER` dangerous?
cards.a:
The driver gets raw, unchecked user addresses

They may be invalid, point into the kernel, or change while being read. The I/O manager does no checking, so the driver must probe and capture everything itself, and every mistake becomes a kernel vulnerability.

cards.q: Why must `count * size` checks be written as `count > room / size`?
cards.a:
The multiplication can overflow; the division cannot

With a huge `count`, `count * size` wraps round to a small value and the check passes, then the driver writes far past the buffer. Dividing the known-good `room` cannot overflow.

cards.q: What is a double-fetch bug?
cards.a:
Reading a user value twice, so it changes after the check

User memory can be changed by another thread at any moment, between the check and the use. Capture the value once into kernel memory, then check and use that copy.

cards.q: Why set `Information` to 0 when failing a request?
cards.a:
So that no uninitialised kernel bytes are copied back to user mode

The I/O manager uses `Information` to decide how many bytes of the system buffer to copy back. On failure there is nothing valid to return, and a stale count risks handing leftover kernel data to the caller.

cards.q: When must a driver use non-paged pool?
cards.a:
When the memory is touched at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` or above

For example in a DPC or while holding a spin lock. Paged pool can be written out to disk, and a page fault cannot be handled at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`.

cards.q: Why does the tag `'nriC'` show up as `Cirn` in PoolMon?
cards.a:
The constant is stored little-endian, so it reads reversed

The compiler makes `'nriC'` a 32-bit number with `'n'` in the top byte. Stored little-endian, the bytes in memory read `C i r n`, which is what PoolMon prints.

cards.q: Why is a big local array dangerous in a driver?
cards.a:
Kernel stacks are only about 12 KB, so a large local can overflow the stack and crash the machine

User-mode threads get 1 MB of stack; kernel threads get a few pages. Allocate big buffers from pool instead.

cards.q: Why can code at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` not wait?
cards.a:
The scheduler cannot run on that processor

The scheduler itself runs at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`. Code already at that level blocks it, so there is nothing to switch to while waiting.

cards.q: Why can code at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` not touch paged memory?
cards.a:
A page fault would have to wait for the disk

Waiting is impossible at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`. Touching resident paged memory happens to work, which hides the bug in testing; when the page is out, the machine bug-checks with `0xD1` or `0x0A`.

cards.q: How do you find the highest IRQL at which a function may be called?
cards.a:
The IRQL line at the end of its documentation (and its `_IRQL_requires_max_` annotation)

Each function's documentation states its IRQL requirement explicitly, and the header's annotation lets static analysis check it. A crash test proves nothing when the page happens to be resident.

cards.q: Why must spin locks be held only briefly?
cards.a:
Waiting processors spin at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`, doing nothing

A waiting processor busy-waits at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`, wasting CPU and unable to run other threads, so long hold times hurt the whole machine.

cards.q: Which lock would you choose for data used by a DPC and a dispatch routine?
cards.a:
A spin lock (preferably queued), because the DPC runs at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` where waiting is impossible

Fast mutexes and executive resources wait, which a DPC cannot do. A DPC can run on another processor at the same moment as the dispatch routine, so the data does need a lock.

cards.q: What does deadlock detection look for?
cards.a:
Two code paths taking the same locks in opposite orders

Lock A then B in one place and B then A in another form a cycle: each path can hold one lock and wait for the other forever. One fixed lock order rules it out.

cards.q: At which IRQL does a DPC run, and what does that forbid?
cards.a:
`DISPATCH_LEVEL`: no waiting and no touching paged memory

DPCs run at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`, so they follow the same two big rules. To do work that needs waiting or paged memory, queue a work item.

cards.q: What does a negative due time in `KeSetTimerEx` mean?
cards.a:
A time relative to now, in 100-nanosecond units

Positive due times are absolute system times; negative ones are relative. Both count in 100 ns units, so one second is -10 000 000.

cards.q: Why must Unload call `KeFlushQueuedDpcs` after cancelling timers?
cards.a:
A DPC may still be queued or running, and it waits for it

`KeCancelTimer` stops future expirations but cannot recall a DPC that is already queued or executing on another processor. Flushing waits until none are left, so none runs in unloaded code.

cards.q: What does `CONTAINING_RECORD` do?
cards.a:
Gets the structure's address from its `LIST_ENTRY`'s address

It subtracts the member's offset from the member's address, giving the start of the containing structure. No search and no copy is involved.

cards.q: How do you know an intrusive circular list is empty?
cards.a:
The head's `Flink` points to the head itself

In a circular list with a head node, an empty list is the head linked to itself; `IsListEmpty` checks exactly that. There are no null pointers in such a list.

cards.q: Why are intrusive lists well suited to the kernel?
cards.a:
Inserting and removing never allocate, so they cannot fail and work under a spin lock

The links live inside the objects, which are already allocated. List operations are only pointer writes, which cannot fail and are fine at `DISPATCH_LEVEL`.

cards.q: What does a null `PPS_CREATE_NOTIFY_INFO` mean in the process callback?
cards.a:
The process is exiting rather than being created

The same callback is used for both events: with creation info for a new process, and with `nullptr` when the process exits.

cards.q: Why must notification callbacks be fast?
cards.a:
Every process and thread creation waits for them

They run synchronously in the creating or exiting thread, so creation cannot carry on until they return. Slow work in them slows the whole system.

cards.q: Why are process ids alone not enough to identify a process in a log?
cards.a:
Ids are reused after a process exits

An id is unique only among the processes alive at one moment. In a log covering hours, the same number can belong to many processes; the start time tells them apart.

cards.q: Why should a driver rate-limit `DbgPrintEx` in hot paths?
cards.a:
Printing is slow and floods the debugger

Formatting and printing a message per event, on every process creation or packet, slows the whole system. Print a summary or every Nth event instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: What do levels and keywords let a trace session do?
cards.a:
Enable only the events of chosen importance and area

The driver checks cheaply whether anyone wants an event before formatting it, so disabled events cost almost nothing. Sessions turn on just the levels and keywords they need.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: What advantage does ETW have over a private log?
cards.a:
Its events appear in system-wide tools like WPA

With ETW you see your driver's events on the same timeline as CPU, disk and other system events, with standard tools to record and view them.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: Why does the read request carry `afterSeq` instead of the driver remembering each reader's position?
cards.a:
The driver then keeps no state for each reader

When the reader says where it is, any number of viewers can read independently, and a crashed viewer leaves nothing behind to clean up.

cards.q: Why is losing events preferable to blocking when the viewer is slow?
cards.a:
Blocking would stall process creation system-wide

The callbacks run in every process creation. Making them wait for a viewer would slow or hang the system; overwriting the oldest entries, and reporting how many were missed, only affects the log.

cards.q: What must Unload do first?
cards.a:
Unregister the callbacks, so no new events arrive

As long as a callback is registered, it can run and write into the ring that is about to be freed. Only once they are unregistered is it safe to tear down the rest, in reverse order.

cards.q: How does special pool catch a buffer overrun at the moment it happens?
cards.a:
Each allocation sits right against an inaccessible page

The first byte past the end lands on the guard page and faults at that instruction. Guard bytes, by contrast, only show the damage later, at free time.

cards.q: Why does Force IRQL checking make paged-memory bugs reproducible?
cards.a:
It pages pageable memory out whenever the IRQL is raised

Normally a paged access at `DISPATCH_LEVEL` crashes only if the page happens to be out. Forcing it out means every bad access faults, on every run.

cards.q: What does low resources simulation test?
cards.a:
The failure paths after allocations, by making random allocations fail

Allocation failures are rare in normal testing, so the code that handles them is rarely run. Making some allocations fail exercises exactly that code.

cards.q: What does `_IRQL_requires_max_(DISPATCH_LEVEL)` let analysis check?
cards.a:
That the function is never called at an IRQL above `DISPATCH_LEVEL`

The annotation states the function's requirement, and static analysis checks every call site against it. It does not change the IRQL itself.

cards.q: Why write driver logic as kernel-independent C++?
cards.a:
So it can be tested and fuzzed quickly in user mode

A crash in a user-mode test is a failed test, not a blue screen, and tests run in seconds. Only a thin kernel layer is left to review, which is how the practice tasks in this course work.

cards.q: What is the difference between generation and mutation fuzzing?
cards.a:
Generation builds inputs from the protocol's description; mutation changes valid inputs randomly

Generation knows the format and can reach deep checks; mutation needs only some valid samples to start from. Good fuzzing often uses both.

cards.q: Why is a generic "read memory at this address" IOCTL a serious flaw?
cards.a:
Anyone who can open the device can read kernel memory

A driver acts with full kernel privilege. Exposing raw memory access hands that privilege to whoever can open the device, turning the driver into a tool against the whole system.

cards.q: What does `FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN` protect against?
cards.a:
Opens of names below the device that skip its security

Without it, a path such as `\\.\Device\anything` below the device name can be opened without the device's own security descriptor being checked. The flag applies the device's security to every such open.

cards.q: Why should a driver never return kernel pointers to user mode?
cards.a:
They reveal the kernel's layout and defeat KASLR

Kernel address randomisation hides where kernel code and data are. One leaked pointer gives that away and makes other bugs much easier to exploit.

cards.q: Why can a developer's own certificate not sign a kernel driver for release?
cards.a:
Release kernel drivers must be signed by Microsoft

Since Windows 10 1607, release kernel drivers need Microsoft's signature, obtained through the Partner Center by attestation or HLK testing. Test signing in a VM is only a development setting.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver

cards.q: What does `DriverVer` in an INF decide?
cards.a:
Which of several driver packages Windows prefers, by date and version

When several packages match a device, Windows ranks them, and `DriverVer`'s date and version decide between otherwise equal candidates.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver

cards.q: How could the log driver's information be obtained without a driver?
cards.a:
By a user-mode program reading the kernel's ETW process and thread events

The kernel already publishes process and thread start and exit events through ETW. A user-mode consumer can read them, with no driver to write, sign or crash.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
